title: Diagnose customer-path dependency timeouts without changing healthy layers
trigger: A customer-facing API request returns HTTP 504 or times out while general service readiness may remain healthy.
preconditions: capture the affected route, customer scope, release version, HTTP status, duration, and X-Request-ID
confirm whether the request reaches the application layer
check readiness and core dependency health before changing any component
identify the downstream dependency and documented application timeout budget
use a direct dependency probe only when it is safe and does not mutate business data
diagnostic_steps: compare the failing customer transaction with /health/ready and direct health endpoints
correlate the X-Request-ID through Nginx and API logs
look for dependency_timeout or equivalent application evidence
probe the suspected downstream service directly using a client timeout larger than the application budget
record both reachability and measured dependency latency
confirm Loki and Tempo correlation for the customer request
distinguish slow-but-reachable service behavior from DNS failure, connection refusal, application exception, or proxy timeout
mitigation_steps: do not restart PostgreSQL, Redis, RabbitMQ, Nginx, or the API when evidence shows they are healthy
do not increase application timeouts during an incident without understanding customer and capacity impact
coordinate recovery with the downstream service owner when latency is the proven fault domain
use application fallback, traffic reduction, or rollback only when an approved design/runbook explicitly supports it
retain request IDs, latency measurements, logs, traces, and dependency-owner communication
validation_steps: re-probe the downstream service and confirm latency is below the application timeout budget
re-test the exact customer request that previously failed
confirm the same application release is still running when no rollback was required
confirm readiness and core dependency health remain healthy
attach an escalation package when the dependency latency cause requires another team or a permanent resilience change
escalation_boundary: Escalate to the downstream service owner when direct evidence proves excessive dependency latency. Escalate to application development when timeout policy, retry/fallback behavior, or code changes are required. Escalate to incident command/platform when multiple services degrade simultaneously, capacity is uncertain, the timeout affects a broad customer population, or safe mitigation is not covered by an approved runbook.
